response:
Here's a defect-by-defect review. I found real problems in all three claims — none of them support the recommendation attached to them.

## Claim 1: "Webinars cause higher retention → make attendance mandatory"

**A. Correlation treated as causation (self-selection).** Customers who choose to attend an optional webinar are almost certainly different from those who don't — more engaged, more invested, more organized — before the webinar ever happens. That same underlying engagement could independently drive retention. Nothing in a simple two-group comparison rules this out. *Effect: the 31% gap may have nothing to do with webinar content at all, so mandating attendance may not move retention at all.*

**B. Survivorship bias in the sample definition.** The population is "customers still active on the Pro plan today" — i.e., churned customers were excluded from the analysis *before* the comparison was even made. When the outcome you care about is retention/churn, conditioning your sample on already having survived is selecting on the dependent variable. *Effect: this can inflate, deflate, or even reverse the true relationship between webinar attendance and churn, because the customers who would most inform the answer (the ones who already left) are missing.*

**C. Immortal time bias.** Attending "at least one onboarding webinar" takes calendar time. A customer who churns in week one never had the opportunity to attend, while a customer who stays six months had many chances to. This mechanically links "attended a webinar" with "survived long enough to attend one," independent of any real effect of the webinar. *Effect: inflates the apparent retention benefit of webinars even if webinars do nothing.*

**D. Voluntary-to-mandatory extrapolation.** Even granting a genuine effect, it was produced by people who *chose* to attend. Forcing attendance on everyone changes the population (including unmotivated, disengaged customers) and may not reproduce the same benefit — compulsory attendance could even annoy customers. *Effect: the policy recommendation doesn't follow from the data used to justify it.*

**E. Population mismatch.** The data is drawn from existing Pro customers, but the recommendation targets *new* Pro customers, an untested population. *Effect: assumes external validity that hasn't been established.*

## Claim 2: "Central region churns less (p=0.04) → concentrate spend there"

**F. Multiple comparisons / data dredging.** Eighteen attributes were tested against churn at a conventional significance threshold. With 18 independent tests at α=0.05, the expected number of false positives by chance alone is ~0.9 — almost exactly one. Finding exactly one "significant" result out of 18 is precisely what pure noise would produce; no correction (Bonferroni, FDR, etc.) was applied. *Effect: the Central-region finding is very likely a false positive, and the memo can't distinguish it from random chance.*

**G. No causal mechanism for the recommended action.** Even if the regional churn difference is real, that says nothing about whether *spending more* in that region would cause further improvement — the analysis found a correlation with churn, not a spend-responsiveness relationship. *Effect: budget could be reallocated based on a lever that was never actually tested.*

**H. Non-sequitur resource-allocation logic.** Even taking the finding at face value, "this region already retains customers well" doesn't imply "invest more there" — it could equally argue for investing in the higher-churn regions that need the help, or that Central needs *less* spend precisely because it's already performing well. *Effect: the recommended action isn't actually supported by the finding, independent of the statistics problem above.*

## Claim 3: "Satisfaction rose 62%→66% → the new support model is working"

**I. No control group or ruling-out of confounds.** A single before/after comparison can't attribute a change to one specific intervention (the new support model) versus seasonality, pricing changes, product changes, or any other concurrent factor. *Effect: credits the support model for a change that may be due to something else entirely, or nothing in particular.*

**J. No significance/uncertainty reported.** There's no confidence interval, sample size, or significance test for the satisfaction survey. A 4-point move in a survey metric can easily be within normal sampling noise. *Effect: may be treating random quarter-to-quarter fluctuation as a real, meaningful improvement.*

**K. Regression to the mean unaddressed.** If last quarter's 62% was itself a low outlier, some rebound toward the average would be expected regardless of any support-model change. *Effect: same as above — overattributes a plausibly mechanical statistical rebound to the intervention.*

**L. Percentage points reported as "%".** Going from 62% to 66% is a 4 *percentage-point* increase, not a "4% improvement" (the actual relative increase is about 6.5%). Not a wrong number, but a description that can mislead a reader about the size of the effect. *Effect: minor, but compounds the impression of a bigger/more definitive change than the data show.*

## Pattern across all three
Every conclusion in the memo jumps from an observational association (or a single pre/post snapshot) straight to a causal claim and a resourcing decision, with no experiment, control group, or correction for known statistical pitfalls (selection bias, immortal time bias, multiple comparisons, lack of a control). The individual numbers may be correct, but none of the three recommendations is actually licensed by the analysis described.
